title: The Mirror of Courtly Truth (KN)
summary: Akbar asks why courtiers constantly flatter him, while Birbal speaks blunt truths. Birbal uses a looking glass to illustrate the nature of mirrors.
full_text:
During an imperial banquet, Emperor Akbar noticed that whenever he expressed an opinion—whether about art, poetry, or war—every courtier enthusiastically agreed, praising the monarch's divine insight. Only Birbal occasionally offered polite dissent or suggested caution.

Later in private chambers, Akbar asked: 'Birbal, why do forty ministers agree with me on everything, while you alone point out flaws in my decrees? Do they respect me more than you do?'

Birbal smiled, walked to an ornamental table, and picked up an exquisite silver looking-glass.

Birbal held the mirror before Akbar's face: 'Sire, what does this mirror do when you look into it?'

Akbar replied: 'It shows my face exactly as it is.'

'If you have a smudge of soot on your cheek, does the mirror conceal it?'

'No,' Akbar said. 'It shows the soot clearly so that I may wash it away.'

Birbal then pulled out a painted miniature portrait of Akbar, crafted by a court artist, depicting the Emperor with smooth, youthful skin, towering height, and a radiant golden halo.

Birbal said: 'Sire, this painted portrait is like your flattering courtiers. It paints what you wish to see, hides every blemish, and tells you that you are flawless. It flatters your vanity, but if you have a speck of soot on your face, it will never warn you!

'I, however, choose to be your looking-glass. A true counselor does not flatter; he holds up the unsparing mirror of truth so that his Emperor may see every smudge of injustice and wash it away before his subjects suffer.

'Those who flatter you love your power and gifts. But he who tells you the honest truth loves your honor and your soul.'

Akbar embraced Birbal with tears of gratitude, declaring that an emperor's greatest treasure is a friend who dares to be a mirror.
